questions.explanation: Weight savings are minimal and do not justify alloy selection; structural loading is dominated by other factors. Cost favors 6063 due to higher extrusion volumes; 5005 is reserved for corrosion-critical applications. Both 5005 and 6063 require anodizing or powder coating to achieve acceptable durability in exposed environments. 5005 (Al-Mg) alloys provide superior corrosion resistance due to the stabilizing effect of magnesium. For severe marine exposure (salt spray, high humidity, low rainfall washoff), 5005 is preferred over 6063. Both still require Type II or Type III anodizing for durability.

questions.text: What is the minimum ultimate tensile strength of 6063-T6 aluminum alloy?
questions.rationale: Per ASTM B221 and the Aluminum Association, 6063-T6 extrusions have a minimum ultimate tensile strength of 190 MPa (typical ~241 MPa). The 186 MPa value belongs to 6063-T5, not T6, and is a common exam trap. 90 MPa is roughly the tensile strength of commercially pure aluminum (1100), and 145 MPa sits in the 6063-T5 typical range. Source: ASTM B221 (https://www.astm.org/b0221-02.html); Aluminum Association material specs.
questions.explanation: 90 MPa is the tensile strength of 1100 (commercially pure aluminum), unsuitable for structural applications. 140 MPa is the minimum tensile strength of 6063-T5, which offers cost savings for non-structural trim. 160 MPa is the yield strength of 6063-T6, not its ultimate tensile strength. 6063-T6 achieves a minimum ultimate tensile strength of 186 MPa, making it suitable for load-bearing architectural members. 6063-T5 typical tensile strength range is 145–186 MPa (not minimum 140 MPa).

questions.text: What gives aluminum its natural corrosion resistance in the checked Metals Lecture?

options.text: A transparent aluminum oxide film on the surface

questions.rationale: The Metals Lecture states that aluminum combines with oxygen to form a transparent aluminum oxide film that makes it corrosion resistant.
questions.explanation: Anodizing protects the aluminum surface but does not prevent galvanic corrosion at contact points where the oxide film is penetrated. Copper and stainless steel are more cathodic than aluminum; they accelerate galvanic corrosion, not inhibit it. Galvanic corrosion occurs between any dissimilar metals in an electrolyte (wet environment), regardless of ferrous/non-ferrous classification. Aluminum is more active (anodic) than stainless steel and copper (both cathodic). Direct contact without isolation creates galvanic cells; aluminum corrodes preferentially. Prevention requires EPDM gaskets, nylon washers, or non-conductive spacers at all metal interfaces.

questions.text: Anodized aluminum finish is best described from the checked source as:

options.text: An electrolytic finish based on aluminum forming a protective oxide coating

questions.rationale: The Metals Lecture describes anodized finishes as electrolytic finishes based on aluminum developing a protective oxide coating.
questions.explanation: Type I (chromic acid) produces only thin films (5–10 µm) with limited corrosion protection—inadequate for exposed architectural work. Both Type I and Type II can achieve color uniformity; the distinction is film thickness and durability, not aesthetics. Cost is not the primary driver; corrosion protection is. Type II's superior film thickness justifies its standard use in architecture. Type II produces a medium-thickness oxide film (10–25 µm) that provides excellent corrosion resistance and aesthetic appearance. This is the standard choice for architectural extrusions exposed to weathering.

questions.rationale: The repaired cluster is limited to source-checked non-ferrous metal definitions, uses, finishes, and galvanic cautions.
questions.explanation: Anodizing provides excellent corrosion protection but offers limited color choices (natural aluminum or dyed colors within the oxide film). Powder coating requires thorough surface preparation (cleaning, conversion coating) to achieve adhesion; skipping this step causes failure. Performance differs; powder coating typically outperforms anodizing in severe coastal/industrial environments and custom color applications. Powder coating applies thermosetting polymers electrostatically and cures through heat, offering superior adhesion, durability, color retention, and uniform coverage. Custom colors and finishes far exceed anodizing capabilities. Both are valid; selection depends on performance and aesthetic requirements.
